text: It is almost midnight. Your spreadsheet is broken, and the deadline is close. You paste the problem into a chatbot. A formula appears. You copy it into the sheet, and the missing result finally arrives.
visual: Night desk assembled from notebook scraps; photographed hand, laptop cutout, clock, spreadsheet grid; identifiable ChatGPT badge redrawn as printed paper.

text: You read the explanation. Every step seems clear. The right column, the right comparison, the right answer. You close the laptop feeling that tomorrow, you could do this yourself. For now, the deadline is safe.
visual: Formula strips stack in order; confident learner cutout and stamped DONE; warm paper shadows, no invented measured score.

text: The next morning, someone changes the table. The value you need is in another column. This time, close the chat window and rebuild the formula. Where would you start? What would you check if it failed?
visual: Same learner and desk in daylight; rearranged spreadsheet columns; chat paper folds shut; blank formula strip remains.

text: That pause is the subject of this film. Does artificial intelligence help you learn, or just finish? A completed task tells you what happened with support. It does not settle what you can do without it.
visual: Large torn-paper title; completed page separates from learner silhouette; title hierarchy follows reference film.

text: The spreadsheet story is an illustration, not a report about a particular person. But the distinction behind it matters in real experiments. Researchers can measure several outcomes that an impressive finished answer leaves unresolved.
visual: Illustrative desk pulls back into research notebook; four blank tabs enter one at a time.

text: Start with assisted performance: can you finish while the tool is available? Then ask about independent performance: can you do it alone? A correct answer on the first test may conceal trouble on the second.
visual: Two physical paper gauges: WITH HELP and ALONE. Same problem remains; chatbot card slides away.

text: Retention adds time. Can you still retrieve the method later? Transfer changes the problem. Can you adapt the idea when the numbers, constraints, or situation are different? These questions deserve their own observations.
visual: Calendar cutout advances; second card changes a spreadsheet table; RETENTION and TRANSFER tabs join.

text: A test immediately after practice cannot establish what someone remembers months later. A repeated question cannot establish performance on every new problem. Before accepting a claim about learning, look at what the researchers actually tested.
visual: Immediate test ticket, long calendar strip and changed problem connected with separate paths; no universal learning score.

text: Smooth reading can make an explanation feel well learned. Producing that explanation with the page covered asks something else. The feeling of access now is useful information, but it is not a guarantee of access later.
visual: Eye follows a printed equation; paper cover slides across it; pencil hesitates at a blank notebook.

text: A field experiment in Turkey makes the distinction unusually clear. Nearly a thousand high school mathematics students took part. Classes received ordinary study resources, an unrestricted chatbot, or a tutor designed with safeguards for learning.
visual: Recognizable Turkish red flag with white crescent and star; classroom collage; three research arms labeled CONTROL, GPT BASE, GPT TUTOR.

text: Both tools used the same underlying model. The unrestricted version resembled a standard chat interface. The guarded tutor drew on teacher prepared solutions and hints, with instructions intended to guide students instead of simply supplying the answer.
visual: GPT-4 printed badge branches into two different paper interfaces; teacher hint cards feed only the tutor branch.

text: During practice, grades rose forty eight percent with the unrestricted chatbot and one hundred twenty seven percent with the guarded tutor, relative to the control group. On that scoreboard, both tools looked highly effective.
visual: Separate practice scoreboard with +48% and +127%, clearly labeled RELATIVE TO CONTROL; avoid inventing raw grades.

text: Then the support disappeared. On the subsequent exam without resources, the unrestricted group scored seventeen percent below the control group. The same intervention had improved assisted work while weakening performance on the test without help.
visual: Chat windows physically pulled from the desk; exam paper revealed; −17% result on independent scoreboard, distinct from practice.

text: Those percentages are relative changes, not percentage points. And the guarded tutor tells another part of the story: its later penalty largely disappeared. Its exam result was not statistically distinguishable from the control group.
visual: Percent label tears away from PERCENTAGE POINTS; tutor exam card sits near control with NO CLEAR DIFFERENCE label.

text: That means the experiment did not establish a positive exam gain for the guarded tutor. It also did not prove the two groups were identical. Preventing an observed loss and demonstrating an improvement are different findings.
visual: Three paper stamps: LOSS, NO CLEAR DIFFERENCE, GAIN. Middle stamp stays visible; no equality sign between groups.

text: Chat logs showed more requests for complete solutions with the unrestricted tool, and more help seeking and attempted answers with the tutor. Those patterns help interpret the result; they do not isolate every possible cause.
visual: Two streams of chat scraps: complete answers versus attempt-and-hint exchanges; paper arrows stop at interpretation note.

text: This was one subject, one school setting, and a short term exam. It was not a test of permanent damage or years of forgetting. Nor did the unrestricted interface force every student to use the same strategy.
visual: Turkey classroom card framed by SUBJECT, SETTING, SHORT TERM labels; long calendar remains outside measured boundary.

text: Now consider college physics. In a separate randomized experiment at Harvard, a carefully designed tutor produced higher immediate test scores than an active classroom lesson. The comparison was with active teaching, not simply watching a passive lecture.
visual: Harvard name and recognizable crimson shield redrawn in collage; physics book and active classroom on parallel paper panels.

text: The tutor used a planned sequence, expert prepared content, questions, feedback, and self pacing. The median post-test score was four point five, compared with three point five in the classroom condition. Teaching design changed the result.
visual: Sequential paper questions, teacher notes and response cards; median score marks 4.5 and 3.5 with IMMEDIATE POST-TEST label.

text: That is encouraging evidence for this instructional system. The assessment still happened immediately after learning. It cannot tell us what those students remembered months later, or what every general chatbot conversation would accomplish.
visual: Harvard study paper clipped to immediate clock; months-later calendar shown as an unanswered empty field.

text: Another randomized mathematics study compared generated help, human tutor help, and no help. Generated help improved learning over no help. The difference from human authored help was not statistically significant, but correctness required careful quality control.
visual: Three mathematics workbooks; ChatGPT badge on generated help, human pen on authored help; compare results without declaring exact equivalence.

text: Thirty two percent of the initially generated help failed the researchers’ quality checks. A confident explanation can still contain incorrect reasoning. A useful tutor needs both a sensible teaching approach and content that can survive checking.
visual: One hundred small paper hint tiles, thirty two marked rejected; wrong multiplication crossed out and corrected.

text: These results point toward a practical question: what thinking remains yours? Cognitive offloading means moving some mental work into an external aid. A calendar, a calculator, a written note, and a chatbot can all play that role.
visual: Vintage calendar, calculator, note and chatbot assembled around learner head; individual cognitive tasks shown as removable paper pieces.

text: Offloading can be sensible. If a formula is routine bookkeeping, having a tool handle it may be exactly what you need. If choosing and checking the formula is the skill you want, outsourcing those steps removes opportunities to practise.
visual: Two task tickets: FINISH BOOKKEEPING and LEARN THE METHOD. Formula choice stays beside learner on the second.

text: The target matters. You might be learning how to select a method, spot an error, or explain why an operation works. Name that target before deciding which part of the work you want the assistant to take over.
visual: Three tangible notebook tabs: CHOOSE, CHECK, EXPLAIN; learner moves only a separate clerical card toward the computer.

text: A preregistered experiment with seven hundred four adults tested feedback about help seeking during fraction arithmetic. Feedback reduced requests for complete answers and improved a later unaided test. The researchers found no evidence that effort rewards changed either outcome.
visual: Fraction cards and personal help-history tally; PREPRINT label; answer requests shrink after feedback, no odds-ratio animation.

text: That study is a recent preprint on a narrow task. It does not establish a universal remedy or years of skill loss. It does suggest that noticing how you seek help can change both behavior and subsequent performance.
visual: Preprint sheet stays visibly provisional; learner reviews personal tally; later small test appears, bounded to fraction arithmetic.

text: Retrieval practice offers another useful test: produce the answer while it is hidden, then check it. A review of forty four studies compared retrieval with other substantial learning activities. Its advantage depended on the comparison and on corrective feedback.
visual: Covered answer, handwritten attempt and correction layered in order; 44-study review card; feedback paper links to attempt.

text: Without checking, you may become fluent at repeating your own mistake. After recall, compare the missing step with a reliable example. For a calculation, substitute the result back. For an explanation, check whether the causal links actually hold.
visual: Incorrect equation strip repeated then stopped; checked substitution replaces it; CHECK card lands after RECALL.

text: But beginners should not have to invent every procedure. In a randomized study of novice secondary students learning algebraic brackets, worked examples beat unguided problem solving on tests taken just after learning, including similar new problems.
visual: Recognizable Indonesian red-over-white flag; novice learner studies complete bracket expansion; original and near-transfer sheets.

text: Trying first also has evidence. A meta-analysis of fifty three studies favored problem solving followed by instruction overall, with differences across ages, tasks, and implementation. It studied teaching sequences, not one universal rule for talking to a chatbot.
visual: Two instructional sequences built from paper arrows; 53-study stack; age and task tabs interrupt universal ranking.

text: A later test can change the picture again. A twenty twenty six working paper studied over six thousand middle-school students, comparing artificial intelligence support with conventional computer practice and varying whether students had to demonstrate mastery.
visual: United States flag as accurate collage; school notebook labeled WORKING PAPER 2026; AI support and conventional practice branches.

text: One week later, students faced practiced and unpracticed material. The delayed benefit was limited and conditional: the most encouraging result appeared within the mastery workflow, on practiced material, and was only marginally statistically significant.
visual: Seven calendar leaves; practiced and unfamiliar questions separated; modest conditional result, no triumphant universal gain graphic.

text: Do not combine those studies into one universal scoreboard. A short term Turkish mathematics exam, an immediate college physics test, and a delayed middle-school assessment ask different questions. Keep the learners, the comparison, and the test in view.
visual: Three research postcards stay separate: Turkey, Harvard, one-week school study. A common table lists population, comparison and assessment.

text: For your own work, adapt the support to what you already know. Study a complete example when you need one. Finish a partial example as understanding grows. Then attempt a fresh problem without the solution in view.
visual: Complete worked page loses selected lines, then folds away for independent page; same learner anchors continuity.

text: Here is a small learning check. It is an editorial synthesis, not a validated ten-minute protocol. Choose one skill and one manageable problem. If you know enough to start, make an attempt before opening the assistant.
visual: Small practical-check notebook with no countdown prescription; named skill and problem; learner writes first attempt.

text: If the topic is entirely new, study one clear worked example first. If you are stuck on a particular step, show your attempt and ask for a hint or a diagnosis of that step. Keep the request specific.
visual: Two paths: NEW TOPIC leads to example; SPECIFIC GAP leads to one hint. Both return to learner work.

text: For example, suppose two times the quantity x plus three equals fourteen. A hint might ask which operation removes the outside factor. Divide both sides by two, then subtract three. The answer is four.
visual: Original equation 2(x+3)=14 on torn paper; divide-by-two operation applied to both sides; then subtract three; x=4.

text: Put four back into the original brackets. Four plus three is seven; twice seven is fourteen. If you expanded the original as two x plus three, the missing multiplication is the mistake to correct.
visual: Substitution shown unambiguously as 2(4+3)=14. Incorrect 2x+3 crossed out; correct 2x+6 revealed.

text: Cover the worked solution and rebuild the method. Explain why each operation preserves the equation. Remembering the final value is not enough for this goal. You want evidence that you can choose and justify the steps yourself.
visual: Solution sheet covered while original question remains; learner creates operations independently; final value does not appear until reconstruction.

text: Then change the problem: three times the quantity y minus two equals fifteen. The answer is seven. The numbers and sign have changed, but the principle is the same. This is a small check of near transfer.
visual: 3(y−2)=15; y−2=5; y=7; changed numbers highlighted; NEAR TRANSFER label.

text: Return later to another fresh problem. A real delay lets you check retention separately. The studies here do not prescribe one perfect interval. Pick a later occasion that matters for your goal, and keep the earlier solution hidden.
visual: Calendar moves to a later day; sealed earlier solution; fresh notebook problem; no evidence-free exact optimal interval.

text: A full answer can still become a learning resource if you study it, cover it, and test yourself. A hint can still be useless if it is wrong or leaves you guessing. Judge what happens after the help, not its label.
visual: Full answer and hint slips both lead to checkable independent work; neither receives automatic good/bad stamp.

text: Keep a simple record: what you attempted, what help you used, and what you could do alone afterward. When transfer matters, change the problem. When retention matters, add a later attempt. Those observations are more informative than familiarity alone.
visual: Three-column learning log with concrete entries; later-date slip and changed-problem slip appended.

text: Return to the spreadsheet. The first formula saved tonight’s deadline. Tomorrow, close the chat, change the table, and rebuild the solution. If you need help, use it, then make room for another independent attempt.
visual: Opening desk returns; morning light, closed ChatGPT paper tab, changed spreadsheet; learner reconstructs formula.

text: Use artificial intelligence to make that next attempt better. A finished task tells you what you achieved with support. What you can explain, check, and do when the support disappears tells you what remains. That is the result worth testing.
visual: Final collage gathers learner, notebook, calendar and checked fresh problem; closing question WHAT REMAINS? with gentle paper settle.
